abstract: The cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 carries the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, and its inactivation needs to be precisely controlled: shifts of only a few millivolts in steady-state inactivation (SSI), or incomplete pore closure generating a late current, are arrhythmogenic. Inactivation is modulated by both tyrosine phosphorylation and protein-protein interactions, but whether or how the two intersect is unclear. Combining protein semi-synthesis with electrophysiology, biochemistry, fluorometry and molecular dynamics simulations, we control phosphorylation at Y1495 in the DIII-DIV linker and demonstrate how it governs regulation by intracellular fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (iFGFs). We find that iFGFs act through two separable mechanisms: a depolarizing SSI shift of around 16 mV that is switched off by phosphorylation, and a suppression of late current that proceeds regardless of phosphorylation. Only the former requires an intact C-terminal domain/DIII-DIV linker interaction, and both differ between iFGF isoforms. Phosphorylation at Y1495 therefore does not switch off the iFGF interaction but instead redirects its output. Together, this reveals a mode of ion channel regulation in which a single post-translational modification selects between different functional consequences of a protein-protein interaction.
